title: Project 1 meets its first audience, and gets rebuilt
introduction: There were three sessions this week. On Tuesday, each group presented Project 1 to Boyd and the whole class for the first time. The opening and closing sections were reasonably good, but there were some issues with the middle section. This blog post mainly describes how I restructured Project 1 based on that feedback. Finally, a brief mention: on Thursday, Boyd demonstrated 11 p5.js examples, and on Friday I had my first attempt at hand tracking using ml5 with Alice.
related_work: Boyd laid down one rule for this pitch: it was to be a dialogue, not a crit; first explain what each screen was intended to convey, then listen. The picture book, with its colours running away like sand, worked well. One student said it felt like ‘memories of childhood bubbling up and then falling off’. No one took issue with the ending. The problem lay with the three screens in the middle. The four gesture icons were too small; Sam said the page ‘looks more akin to rock, paper, scissors’; Boyd called that a happy accident and told us to use it. The large face seemed too clear for a memory. No one saw the connection between that face and the silhouette of the child that followed it. Boyd said something I had to write down twice: ‘It makes sense when you tell us, but when we experience it ourselves, we’re not connecting the picture to the idea.’ And the most heartbreaking criticism concerned the sixteen memories we had pre-drawn: ‘I wasn’t that little girl, I don’t have that memory.’
method:
On Tuesday evening, I redesigned the middle section, adding more explanatory text to each screen. The result was actually worse. My partner hit the nail on the head: the first version felt like a picture book, whilst the new version read like an instruction manual. We also uncovered a contradiction that no amount of text could resolve: it was simply impossible for two strangers to find their own memories amongst the sixteen pictures we had drawn in advance. So I emailed Boyd proposing two routes. Route A: role play. The boy and the girl in the book are masks; the players wear them and play rock, paper, scissors with real hand signs, and each outcome opens one of our pre-drawn moments. All hand-drawn, and honest about being pre-set. Route B: a short questionnaire answered with hand signs, with the final picture generated by a model, much like the ‘ask the model’ step in Project 0.

The following morning, Boyd replied: carry on in the direction we were heading; we did not need generative AI for anything. He also added four pieces of advice: state the purpose right at the start; blur the faces and ask, ‘Do you remember her?’; give the hand signs a reason; and draw the figures from real, private childhood memories rather than generic ones. This became Version 7. Rock, paper, scissors is the magic that brings a memory back. Three rounds correspond to three days: a summer afternoon, the night of the power cut, and the day she moves away. A win, a draw or a loss opens one of nine scenes: he climbs the mulberry tree while she cries; they spit watermelon seeds over the wall; the kite gets stuck in the tree; he eats the last ice lolly during the power cut; they lie on the roof watching the stars; the removal van turns into the alley; she waves from the back of the van, and he runs after it. I draw every black figure and prop in Piskel; my partner paints the coloured backgrounds. The faces in the dialogue boxes are blurred; each scene has three fixed lines; and the ending returns to the big book: the pages you have unlocked are filled in, the rest stay blank, and the final line reads ‘the memory is not over’. We kept the lines pre-written rather than typed in by the players, so the whole piece stays hand-made and reads as one book.
results_discussion:
Thursday. Boyd gave us a repository containing 11 working p5.js sketches: variables and conditionals, loops, functions, objects, nearest-point search, mapping and easing, pixels as an array, vectors and transforms, 3D with WebGL, a signal over time, and a particle system. In class, we only covered the first four. He asked us to look up the map() function in the reference ourselves and asked, ‘Why is it 20?’ The homework is a bug in the objects sketch: a ball spawned within 30 pixels of the edge gets stuck flipping its direction. Next Tuesday, everyone is to explain how all 11 examples work, and the crit has been rescheduled to 5 November. I have no background in programming, so these examples are quite difficult for me to understand, but I will practise them and work through all 11 before Tuesday.

Friday. Alice introduced ml5.js handPose: the webcam provides twenty-one named points for each hand, such as thumb_tip and index_finger_tip. First came the two coloured dots on the fingertips. Then my own rounds. Round one: Thanos’s gauntlet following my index finger (as it was a JPG, it came with a white box around it; next time I will use a transparent PNG). Round two: five gems, from red to blue, one on each fingertip, which is simply the same image() line repeated five times with a different point name. When Alice leaned in to take a closer look, her hand entered the frame and the gems jumped onto her hand: the program only knows hands[0], the first hand it sees. This is precisely the piece that Project 1 was missing. Rock, paper and scissors can be told apart by counting extended fingers, and these few lines of code will replace the number keys I am using now.
conclusion_future_work: Current progress on Project 1: nine scenes have been drawn or are being drawn; a demo video of the full flow has been produced; Version 6 is still running on the cloud server for classmates to use; and hand tracking has not yet been wired in. The checkpoint is the crit on 5 November. What I learnt this week was not about code: using more words to explain a picture can actually make it worse. The fix lay in structure, and in giving the game a reason.
